title: Rent rises ‘five times Jim’s claim’
full_text:
Property tax changes in the federal budget will stunt housing construction and lower GDP by $1bn over the next four years, according to new modelling by the nation's leading property bodies that also predicts the crackdown will add $10 a week to rents every year, five times more than Jim Chalmers promised.
The updated analysis found the Albanese government’s ban on self-managed super funds borrowing to buy property alongside changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax will likely lead to 10,700 fewer homes being built to 2029-30.
Delivering the budget in May, the Treasurer claimed the changes would direct investors into freshly built stock with the restricted access to negative gearing on new builds.
The modelling – commissioned by the Real Estate Institute of Australia, the Property Council of Australia, Master Builders Australia and the Housing Industry Association – estimated that the disincentives were exacerbated by the Albanese government’s deal with the Greens to pass the budget Of the 10,700 fewer homes, the modelling attributed about 2000 to the SMSF changes negotiated with the Greens in the Senate. No modelling was completed to assess the potential market impact of this policy.
Less housing stock will compound pressure on the already stretched rental market and push rents up $10 a week each year, separate to inflation, the modelling concluded. It dismissed the $2 weekly figure modelled by Treasury and used by Dr Chalmers to sell the budget.
In a joint statement, the four property groups said the SMSF changes would push the Housing Accord targets of 1.2 million new homes by mid-2029 further out of reach. “The updated figures reinforce a straightforward point: Australia cannot resolve its housing shortage through policies that make it harder to finance, build, and supply rental homes,” the statement said.
The modelling by Qaive and Tulipwood Economics, to be released on Friday, suggests the drop in new construction will lead to 4700 fewer jobs in the sector and could put additional pressure on inflation.
Tulipwood Economics director Joe Branigan said the SMSF ban removed a source of finance from a market in desperate need of more investment.
“Our modelling for the REIA finds the SMSF measure on its own takes close to 2000 dwellings and more than 800 construction jobs out of the pipeline between 2026-27 and 2029-30, reduces GDP by almost $200m, and adds around $1.15 a week to average rents,” Mr Branigan said.
“The federal government says it wants more homes and cheaper rents, but its own policy choices are pushing Australia towards fewer homes and higher rents. You cannot fix a housing shortage with measures that make it harder to finance the homes that need to be built.“ The new figures paint a bleaker picture of the budget fallout than previously predicted, revising rent expectations up from $9 weekly rises by the end of the decade.
Master Builders chief executive Denita Wawn said the federal government must consider reversing the changes. “It is incredibly difficult to make any investment in housing stack up at the moment, and our concern is … we are going backwards in our capacity to build, which is only going to exacerbate an already difficult situation for all Australians around the country,” she said.
The Housing Industry Association believes fallout from the changes could be larger than that modelled by Tulipwood, with the body’s chief economist Tim Reardon suggesting 40,000 fewer homes would be built over the coming decade – 5000 more than Labor’s modelling.
“Increasing the supply of new homes is now a macroeconomic policy constraint,” Mr Reardon said. “The restriction of places on the ability of free movement of labour, as well as the cost it imposes on employment, means that it is not just a social issue going ahead.” Real Estate Institute of Australia president Jacob Caine said the modelling was a “clear warning” that the budget policies would deepen the housing shortage.
“Almost 10,700 fewer homes, higher rents, and a billion-dollar hit to economic activity is the opposite of what Australians need during a housing crisis,” Mr Caine said. “Every housing policy should pass one basic test: will it help build more homes?” A spokesman for Dr Chalmers said the budget showed a small impact on rents over time. “Treasury’s assumptions in the Budget show a small impact on rents, which is expected over time, not overnight,” he said. “There is a lot of factors that go into rents, as there are for house prices, with underlying supply and demand a key factor and our policies will add to housing supply by over 30,000 homes over the next 10 years, putting downward pressure on rents over time.” Opposition Treasury spokesman Andrew Bragg said it was “nonsensical” that the Albanese government would stop SMSF purchases during a housing crisis. “The ban on SMSFs was an insane idea because, by definition, the owners can’t live in the houses, so it was always going to create a hit to rents,” Senator Bragg said.
